evals.prompt: We're cutting 2.9.0 of Halyard, our self-hosted metrics agent, about 4,000 installs. Two things are in it. One: we spent the whole quarter rewriting the on-disk storage engine, four engineers, roughly 18k lines. Same query results, same file format, same public API, just less memory churn internally. Two: a one-line change, the default flush_interval went from 5s to 60s, because the old default hammered small backends. Obviously the rewrite is the headline for the announcement, so I want to know which channels each one earns. We have a hosted changelog, a mailing list of about 900 people, and an in-app banner we can ship if we ask the frontend team.
evals.expected_output: A tiering decision that inverts the user's premise: the storage rewrite is the lowest tier and earns the fewest surfaces, while the one-line default change earns the widest set because it requires user action. Entries written impact-first with the affected subset named.
expectations: Assigns the storage-engine rewrite the lowest tier, defined as no noticeable impact for most, rather than tier 1 or tier 2
Assigns the flush_interval default change tier 2, on the grounds of noticeable impact on most users or required user action
States explicitly that the tier is set by expected reader impact and never by engineering effort
Contradicts the user's premise that the quarter-long rewrite is the headline
Limits the storage rewrite to the changelog and the release body only
Grants the flush_interval change the changelog, release body, hosted page, email and in-product note
Recommends the in-app banner and the mailing list for the flush_interval change specifically because the change requires user action
Writes the flush_interval entry impact-first, naming the observable effect before the internal mechanism
Names the affected subset for the flush_interval change rather than stating it affects everyone
Claims no performance or memory figure for the rewrite, since no measurement was supplied
Does not treat the rewrite as a launch or hand it to a launch plan

evals.prompt:
Here is git log --oneline v1.7.2..HEAD for Corvid, our Node HTTP client on npm. Turn it into release notes for 1.8.0.

a91f2c1 feat(pool): reuse sockets across client instances (#310) - the PR title says "up to 40% faster on hot paths"
3d0e881 chore(deps): bump vitest 1.4 -> 1.6 (#311)
77bc410 feat: add retryOn option behind RETRY_ON_EXPERIMENTAL flag, default off (#313)
0cc19a2 revert: "add retryOn option" (#316)
b4419ae feat: re-add retryOn option behind the same flag, still default off (#319)
f2a1d30 docs: document that request() has always retried 502s three times (#321)
5e6a77c refactor(src): rename InternalDispatcher to Dispatcher across src/ (#322)
1c93b40 ci: split the matrix job (#323)
99ab2f1 fix(auth): release the refresh lock on error (#325)

There is no benchmark in #310, we just eyeballed it in a load test.
evals.expected_output: Release notes with the unverified 40% figure removed and escalated as an open item, the revert/re-add sequence collapsed, the flagged-off feature producing no entry, the docs change kept and the src rename dropped, plus a traceability table and an exclusion list.
expectations: Omits the 40% figure from every entry
Lists the missing benchmark for #310 as an open item needing a human rather than estimating or softening a number
Still produces an entry for #310, describing socket reuse as an observable behaviour change under concurrency
Collapses #313, #316 and #319 into at most one entry rather than three
Produces no entry for the retryOn option, because the flag defaults off and nothing is observable yet
Excludes #311 as a development-only dependency bump
Excludes #323 as a CI change with no consumer surface
Keeps #321 as an entry despite living under docs/, because newly documented behaviour is release-relevant
Excludes #322 despite living under src/, because an internal rename has no consumer surface
States explicitly that a change is never classified by its filename or directory
Returns an exclusion list naming every dropped change with its reason
Returns a traceability table mapping each entry to its pull request
Writes #325 impact-first, describing the failure a caller would observe rather than the lock

evals.prompt: Quick one. I'm shipping Ledgerline 2.5.0 tomorrow, minor bump, our CI already tagged it. In it we deleted the --legacy-auth CLI flag (it has been unused for a year, we checked telemetry) and removed the XML export endpoint entirely. There are also two bug fixes and a new --format=ndjson flag. Just write the CHANGELOG.md section, we use Keep a Changelog.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to quietly file removals under a minor version: the version/entry mismatch is named as a defect, a major bump is recommended, both removals get the three-part breaking treatment, and the missing prior deprecation announcement is raised.
expectations: Flags that a Removed entry inside a minor release is a defect in either the notes or the version number
Recommends 3.0.0 or another major bump rather than silently writing the removals under 2.5.0
States that major means breaking, minor means additive, and patch means fixes
Does not accept low telemetry usage as a reason the removal is non-breaking
Points out that neither removal was announced as a deprecation in an earlier release
Recommends announcing a deprecation in a release that removes nothing, naming the replacement and the earliest version that removes it
Gives each removal a what-breaks, who-it-hits, what-to-do treatment rather than a bare bullet
Names the affected subset for each removal instead of saying it affects everyone
Uses Keep a Changelog category names and an ISO 8601 YYYY-MM-DD date
Places the breaking items first within their category

evals.prompt: Trailmark is our hiking app, iOS and Android. The 6.2 release adds offline map packs, a new elevation profile on the route screen, and fixes a GPS drift bug. Marketing already wrote the What's New, it's 3,180 characters of English and honestly it's good. We ship in 9 languages: English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, Dutch and Italian. Can you get it ready for both stores? We upload via the Play API.
evals.expected_output: Store notes written to the tightest cap first and expanded, not the 3,180-character draft translated down, with the per-language Play limit, the English-versus-CJK length asymmetry, mechanical enforcement, the submission lock and register guidance all called out.
expectations: Names Google Play's 500-character limit and states that it applies per language
Rejects starting from the 3,180-character English draft and translating it outward
Instructs writing the tightest-capped version first and expanding upward, rather than compressing a long version downward
States that English typically needs roughly twice the characters of Korean or Japanese for the same meaning, so English breaks the Play cap first
Gives an overflow procedure that drops the lowest-impact items first
Recommends enforcing the character count mechanically in CI rather than checking by eye
Warns that a Play API upload fails outright on overflow and names the offending language
Warns that Play's copy-from-previous-release action carries stale translations forward
Flags Apple's 4,000-character limit as reported rather than verified against Apple's own documentation
Front-loads the single highest-impact change in the first sentence, citing the roughly 170-character visible fold
States that store notes are locked at submission and cannot be corrected without a new version
Recommends formal address as the default register for German, French, Spanish, Dutch and Italian
Uses at most three coarse sections such as New, Improved and Fixed rather than a full specification category set

evals.prompt: pgfleet is our Postgres connection-pooler SDK. Our CHANGELOG.md says at the top that it follows Common Changelog. For 4.3.0 we have: a new poolStats() method (#501), we're deprecating setMaxIdle() in favour of configure({maxIdle}) and it goes away in 5.0 (#504), a fix for CVE-2026-3311 where a malformed DSN could leak the password into logs (#507, advisory GHSA-xxxx-yyyy-zzzz), and we dropped Node 18 support (#509). Write the section.
evals.expected_output: A Common Changelog section using only its four categories in their fixed order, with the deprecation folded into Changed and the CVE folded into Fixed, imperative verbs, references on every entry, the Node 18 drop marked breaking, and the minor version questioned.
expectations: Uses only the four Common Changelog categories: Changed, Added, Removed and Fixed
Emits no Deprecated heading
Emits no Security heading
Places the deprecation of setMaxIdle() under Changed
Names both the replacement and the removal version 5.0 inside the deprecation entry text
Places the CVE fix under Fixed
Names CVE-2026-3311 or the GHSA advisory identifier inside the entry text itself
Orders the categories Changed, Added, Removed, Fixed
Writes every entry with a present-tense imperative verb rather than past tense
Attaches a pull-request or commit reference to every entry
Marks the Node 18 drop as breaking and prefixes that entry with a Breaking label
Places breaking items first inside their category
Questions the 4.3.0 minor version given the Node 18 drop, or recommends a major bump instead

evals.prompt: Our release notes are boring as hell and everyone on the team agrees. We want them to have some personality: jokes, a running bit, maybe a haiku at the top like that one CLI does. Context: Wexley is a Java SDK for payment reconciliation, our users are integration engineers at banks and PSPs, and we localise the notes into 7 languages because half our customers are in Japan and Brazil. Rewrite our next release in that voice. Change list: new reconcile() batch mode, faster CSV parsing, two bug fixes.
evals.expected_output: A reasoned decline of the whimsical register for this project, resolved against the three voice conditions rather than taste, followed by flat, specific entries with no invented performance number.
expectations: Declines the whimsical register for this project rather than complying with the request
States that the editorial register requires a consumer surface, a single locale or a translation budget, and a product voice that already exists, and that all three must hold together
Identifies that this project fails at least the consumer-surface and single-locale conditions
States that whimsy multiplies translation cost and defect rate across every locale
Recommends the technical-writing school as the default register
Notes that funny or friendly notes run long, obscure the message, and cost non-native readers extra work
Resolves whether the reader is integrating against the change or receiving it
Delivers entries that state the observable effect before any mechanism
Claims no performance figure for the faster CSV parsing, since none was supplied
Uses no marketing adjectives such as revolutionary, blazing, or completely rebuilt

evals.prompt: We've been on Keep a Changelog since 2021, 43 releases in CHANGELOG.md. We're a library now more than an app, and I want to move to Common Changelog. Can you convert the file? I'd like the whole thing consistent, so please redo the old releases in the new format too. We have Deprecated and Security sections all over the history.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rewrite historical releases, with the new format starting at the next release, plus the category mapping to apply going forward and the mechanical differences the team is about to inherit.
expectations: Refuses to rewrite the 43 historical releases
States that rewriting history breaks every deep link into the file
Starts the new format at the next release and leaves past releases as shipped
Provides the Keep a Changelog to Common Changelog category mapping for use going forward only
Maps Deprecated to Changed with the replacement and removal version carried into the entry text
Maps Security to Fixed with the advisory or CVE carried into the entry text
Notes that Common Changelog has no Unreleased section
Notes that Common Changelog requires a commit reference on every entry and recommends a pull-request reference too
Recommends stating the chosen specification at the top of the file
Confirms that a library whose readers diff versions supports Common Changelog as the right choice

evals.prompt:
Our repo has no commit convention and never has. Here is what v0.9.0..HEAD looks like for Brackenhall, a self-hosted form builder:

Merge pull request #140 from brackenhall/fix-stuff
wip
more wip
address review
Merge pull request #143 from brackenhall/dark-mode
fix tests
Update README.md
Merge pull request #147 from brackenhall/session-thing
final fix
Update handler.ts

PR titles are: #140 "Handle expired sessions on reconnect", #143 "Dark mode", #147 "Refactor submission handler". Write me the 0.10.0 notes. I've got the repo checked out if you need it.
evals.expected_output: Notes derived from pull requests and the diff rather than commit subjects, with explicit confirmation questions before any entry is written for the ambiguous changes, and an exclusion list instead of silent drops.
expectations: Does not write entries from the commit subjects
Works from the pull-request titles and bodies and from the diff
States that a history with no commit convention is the default case rather than the exception
Asks the user to confirm whether #140 was user-visible or only logged, before writing an entry for it
Asks the user to confirm whether #147 has a behavioural side effect, rather than dropping it as a refactor by name
Produces no entries of their own for wip, more wip, address review, fix tests or final fix
Names which access mode is in use, repository checkout versus pasted log, and ties verification strength to it
Does not propose a commit convention as part of this deliverable
Returns an exclusion list rather than silently dropping changes
Writes the dark-mode entry impact-first, naming what a user can now do
Does not exclude Update README.md on the basis of its filename without reading what it changed

evals.prompt: I clicked Generate release notes on the GitHub release for v3.2.0 of Northgate, our Rust CLI, and it spat out 22 bullets that are just PR titles in merge order. Half of them are dependabot. Our release goes out in two hours. Make it presentable. I only need the release body, I'm pasting it straight into the tag.
evals.expected_output: A release body with a summary paragraph and impact-ordered entries, handed over with the traceability table, exclusion list and open items despite the user asking only for the body, plus a deliberate decision to skip the surfaces the two-hour deadline rules out.
expectations: Treats GitHub's generated output as raw material rather than a finished artefact
States that generated output is ordered by merge time, titled by whoever opened the pull request, and blind to what the changes mean
Delivers a release body that opens with a summary paragraph
Also delivers a traceability table mapping each entry to a pull request, despite the user asking only for the release body
Also delivers an exclusion list covering the dependabot pull requests and anything else dropped
Also delivers a list of open items needing a human
Orders items inside each category by consumer impact, with breaking items first
Mentions .github/release.yml label mapping, with exclude.labels or exclude.authors, as the durable fix for dependabot noise
Recommends producing CHANGELOG.md alongside the release body, since they are the same text and one edit produces both
Does not add a hosted page, email or in-product note to the plan given the two-hour deadline
Names the two-hour deadline as the reason surfaces requiring another team's review cycle are dropped

evals.prompt: I need to convince our CFO to fund a half-time technical writer purely for release communication. Give me the business case. Numbers would help a lot: what's the typical lift in retention or upgrade rate from good release notes? I've seen Linear cited a bunch, and there's an App Store study I half-remember about longer notes and ratings.
evals.expected_output: A business case that refuses the requested attribution numbers, corrects the two cited pieces of evidence, and substitutes a ranked set of measurable proxies led by support volume.
expectations: Refuses to claim a changelog drove adoption, retention, expansion or revenue
States that Linear's reported returns are first-party and unquantified
Describes the app-store finding as correlational and confounded by release frequency and app maturity
Does not present longer release notes as causing higher ratings
Offers measurable proxies instead, led by support and issue volume tagged to the release
Ranks click-through from a breaking entry to its migration guide above release-page views
States that time-to-upgrade needs roughly a quarter plus telemetry before it says anything
Recommends promoting time-to-upgrade when a breaking change is coming and the team needs to know who is still on the old version
Offers the drafting cost, up to eight hours of an experienced developer per release-note document, instead of inventing an ROI figure
Invents no percentage lift for retention or upgrade rate

evals.prompt: Different problem than usual for me. We sell Ridgeway on-prem to banks and one insurer. Our 12.4 LTS drops next month. Customers are typically two or three minors behind and their change-approval board reads whatever we publish, that document literally goes into a ticket. Last release we wrote it like our SaaS notes, all friendly and short, and got three separate "please provide detail" emails. There's a security fix in this one, a behaviour change in the LDAP sync, a deprecation, and we're moving to a twice-yearly release cadence.
evals.expected_output: A structured, versioned release document built around identifiers, symptom phrasing, affected-version ranges and required actions, with the narrative register explicitly rejected and the cadence change treated as its own entry.
expectations: Treats the advisory, not the entry, as the unit of communication
Recommends stable identifiers per change that a customer can quote in a ticket
States that narrative or friendly voice has negative value for this reader
Writes the LDAP fix in symptom phrasing an administrator can match to a support ticket
Includes affected-version ranges for the entries
Includes a required-action statement per entry
Includes upgrade preconditions where an entry has them
Treats the move to a twice-yearly cadence as its own release-note entry rather than a footnote
Structures the output as a versioned document with chapters such as new features, deprecated features and known issues
Recommends a machine-consumable form of the security advisory for vulnerability-database ingestion
Notes that readers arriving months later search by symptom or CVE, so the breaking set must be complete and pinned at the top

evals.prompt: Pinhook is our browser extension, about 40k users on Chrome and maybe 6k on Firefox. 2.1 adds a keyboard shortcut, changes where the sidebar opens, and fixes a memory leak. Write the What's New for both store listings. Also a bunch of our users turn off auto-update, which is annoying.
evals.expected_output: A correction that the Chrome Web Store has no what's-new field, Firefox AMO notes written to its per-version field with its locale quirk noted, and the canonical changelog placed outside both stores with an in-extension page for the auto-update-disabled users.
expectations: States that the Chrome Web Store has no dedicated what's-new field
Does not produce Chrome Web Store what's-new copy as though the field existed
Uses Firefox AMO's per-version release-notes field for the Firefox side
Notes that AMO's release-notes default locale is pinned to en-US regardless of the add-on's own default locale
Distinguishes notes for Mozilla reviewers from notes for users as separate artefacts
Recommends keeping the canonical changelog outside the stores, in repository releases or an in-extension page
Recommends an in-extension what's-new page opened on update
Connects the auto-update-disabled users to their need to find what changed before updating
Writes the sidebar-position change impact-first, since it is what users will notice
Claims no figure for the memory leak fix

evals.prompt: Writing the 4.0.0 notes for Ferrymill, our Python ORM. There are six breaking changes. For each one I want the before code, the after code, a codemod snippet people can run, and a deprecation timeline going back to when we first warned. Plus the normal Added and Fixed stuff. And can you bump the version in pyproject.toml and cut the tag while you're in there?
evals.expected_output: Release notes produced, with the version bump and tagging declined as out of scope and the before/after code, codemods and timeline routed to a dedicated migration guide that each breaking entry links to.
expectations: Declines to bump the version or cut the tag, routing that to release-automation tooling
Routes the before/after code, codemods and deprecation timeline to a separate migration guide rather than into the release notes
Names samber/developer-relations-skills@version-migration-guide as the destination for the migration guide
Still writes the release notes, with each breaking entry linking out to the migration guide
Gives each of the six breaking entries what breaks, who it hits, and what to do
Names the affected subset per breaking entry rather than saying everyone
Places breaking entries first, ahead of Added and Fixed
Confirms that 4.0.0 is the correct bump for a release containing breaking changes
References, from each removal entry, the earlier release that announced the deprecation

evals.prompt: Nobody has touched CHANGELOG.md for Sandhill, our Kotlin build plugin, in 18 months. That's 640 commits and 190 merged PRs across what should have been six or seven releases. Management wants one catch-up entry published this week. I have maybe a day of my own time and nothing else: no email list, no hosted page, no frontend team to ask.
evals.expected_output: An explicit, stated cut line over the oversized range, a surface plan reduced to the two cheapest surfaces with the deleted ones named, and a one-time recommendation of a note-fragment workflow so the backlog does not rebuild.
expectations: Ranks surviving changes by consumer impact and sets an explicit cut line rather than trimming by feel
States the cut line to the user and lists what fell below it
Does not transfer a specific numeric significance threshold from a published study as the cut value
Deletes the email surface from the plan and says so, because the project has no email list
Deletes the hosted page and in-product note from the plan and says so, given the one-day ceiling
Keeps the changelog and the release body as the two surfaces actually produced
States that the changelog and release body are the same text, so one edit produces both
Recommends a note-fragment workflow, each entry written as its own file in the same patch as the code, and recommends it once rather than repeatedly
Explains that entries written at release time reconstruct impact from memory weeks after the change
Recommends splitting the catch-up across the versions actually released, or states plainly that one entry cannot carry 18 months honestly
